descripcion: At C2 you deploy the rarer inversion patterns — Only when, Little did I know, Not only… but also — and combine them with cleft sentences for a sustained argumentative or literary effect across several sentences, not just one.

filas: Only when the results came in did the flaw become clear.
Little did we know what awaited us.
Not only did she finish early, but she also won.
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: These patterns are markers of a literary or highly rhetorical register — using more than one per paragraph in ordinary prose reads as overwrought.

ejemplos.texto: Only when the results came in did the flaw become clear.
Little did we know what awaited us on the other side.
Not only did she finish early, but she also won first prize.

notas: Little did + subject is almost always followed by know, expect, or realise, and signals dramatic irony about a past the reader already understands.
Not only requires do-support in the inverted clause: not only did she finish, not not only she finished.
These are markers of written, often literary or highly rhetorical register — restraint matters more than range here.

contraste.es: Spanish achieves a similar rhetorical effect through free word order and emphatic phrases (fue precisamente entonces cuando…), without obligatory grammatical inversion. Advanced Spanish speakers therefore find it hard to remember that English inversion after these openers is syntactically required, not an optional choice for emphasis.
contraste.de: German fronts almost any element and inverts automatically (Nur dann verstand ich es), so the idea of inversion after a fronted phrase is familiar. The trap is do-support: German has no auxiliary to insert, which produces Little knew I instead of Little did I know, and the English restriction of inversion to negative or restrictive openers is new.
contraste.it: Italian achieves emphasis through free word order and clefts (è stato allora che…), so it-clefts come easily. Grammatical inversion with do-support has no Italian model, and because Italian can place the subject after the verb freely, Italian speakers may invert where English does not allow it.
contraste.fr: French has literary inversion after openers such as à peine or peut-être (À peine était-il arrivé que…), a close model for Hardly had he arrived when…. Clefts (c'est… que) are extremely frequent in French, so French speakers use it-clefts readily, sometimes more often than English prefers.
contraste.pt: Portuguese emphasises through free word order and clefts (foi então que…, o que eu quero é…), so it-clefts and wh-clefts come easily. Inversion with do-support has no Portuguese model and has to be learned as a fixed set of openers.

errores: Omitting do-support after not only in the inverted clause.
Using more than one of these dramatic patterns per paragraph, which reads as overwrought rather than emphatic.
Using little did in a context that isn't retrospective irony.

es: *No solo … sino que* rendered as *Not only he resigned, but that he…* instead of *Not only did he resign, but he also…*.
de: *kaum … als* rendered with *as*: *Hardly had I arrived as the phone rang* instead of *when the phone rang*.
it: *non appena … che* rendered with *that*: *No sooner had I arrived that the phone rang* instead of *than the phone rang*.
fr: *à peine … que* rendered with *that*: *Hardly had I arrived that the phone rang* instead of *when the phone rang*.
pt: *mal* read as *badly*: *Badly had I arrived when…* instead of *Hardly had I arrived when…*.

redemittel.expresion: Two in a row and it turns theatrical.
redemittel.funcion: names the cost of stacking the structures

traducciones.de: Zwei hintereinander und es wirkt theatralisch.
traducciones.fr: Deux de suite et cela devient théâtral.
traducciones.it: Due di fila e diventa teatrale.

mision.consigna: Write a short speech about what really motivates people at work.
requisitos: three rare inversion patterns (*Rarely, if ever*, *Never before had*, *So … was … that*)
one cleft combined with an inversion in the same passage
the devices spread across several sentences
use *autonomy*, *a sense of purpose* and *to be intrinsically motivated*

microtareas.texto: Choose three that work in speech. Drop the rest.
Record 2 minutes on *quiet quitting*: *Only when… did…*

autochequeo: Is do-support present after not only in the inverted clause?
Is little did followed by know, expect or realise, signalling retrospective irony?
Is at most one of these dramatic patterns used per paragraph?
Does the content genuinely justify this level of rhetorical weight?
Would a native reader sense control rather than strain?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the rarer inversion and emphatic structures. Check do-support after not only, and flag any paragraph stacking more than one dramatic pattern. Do not rewrite the text.
